Credit Card Fraud Prediction


Introduction


The dataset contains credit cards transaction by european cardholders in September 2013. This dataset has transactions data that occurred in two days, where there are 492 frauds out of 284807 transactions. The dataset is highly unbalanced, where the positive class (frauds) is 0.172% of all transactions.

Due to confidentiality constraints, it contains only numerical variables which are the result of PCA transformation and doesn't provide the original features.
- Variables V1, V2, ... V28 are the principal components obtained with PCA
- Variables Time and Amount are the only those have not been transfromed with PCA. Feature Time contains the elapsed seconds between eachtransaction and the transaction in the dataset, and feature Amount is the transaction amount.
- Response variables is feature Class and it takes 1 for fraud case and 0 otherwise.

The objective of this project is to predict whether a credit card transaction is fraudulent or non-fraudulent based on anonymized features (V1–V28), transaction time, and transaction amount.

Dataset Source: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mlg-ulb/creditcardfraud

Transactions in time

In [22]:
class_0 = df.loc[df['Class'] == 0]["Time"]
class_1 = df.loc[df['Class'] == 1]["Time"]

hist_data = [class_0, class_1]
group_labels = ['Not Fraud', 'Fraud']

fig = ff.create_distplot(hist_data, group_labels, show_hist=False, show_rug=False)
fig['layout'].update(title='Credit Card Transactions Time Density Plot', xaxis=dict(title='Time [s]'))
iplot(fig, filename='dist_only')
 
Fraudulent transactions are more evenly distributed across time compared to real transactions. While the real transactions cluster during typical business hours, fraudulent transactions occur uniformly thorughout the day and night.
 

Correlation Matrix

In [26]:
plt.figure(figsize = (14,14))
plt.title('Credit Card Transactions features correlation plot (Pearson)')
corr = df.corr()
sns.heatmap(corr,xticklabels=corr.columns,yticklabels=corr.columns,linewidths=.1,cmap="Blues")
plt.show()
 
Based on the above heatmap, there is no notable correlatioan between features V1-V28. There are certain correlation between some of these features and Time (negative correlation with V3) and Amount (positive correlation with V7 and V20, negative correlation with V1 and V5).

From this feature density plot, we can observe a good selectivity in terms of distribution for the two Class: V25, V26, V28 have similar profile for both Class, V2, V3, V10 have a quite different profile, V4, V11 have clearly separated distributions and V12, V14, V18 have partially separated distributions.

Generally, other than Time and Amount, the features distributions for non-fraudulent transactions (Class = 0) is centered around 0, sometime with a long queue at one of the extremities. In the same time, the fraudulent transactions (Class = 1) have a skewed distribution.
 

Data Splitting

In [73]:

y = df['Class']
In [74]:
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42
)
In [75]:
skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
 

Predictive Modelling


We chose tree-based models suitable for imbalanced classification:
- Random Forest
- XGBoost
- LightGBM
- CatBoost

Class imbalance is handled using:
- class_weight='balanced' (Random Forest, LightGBM)
- scale_pos_weight (XGBoost)
- class_weights (CatBoost)

RandomForestClassifier

In [76]:
rf = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=200,
    class_weight='balanced',
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

Random Forest Classification Report: precision recall f1-score support 0 1.00 1.00 1.00 56864 1 0.96 0.76 0.85 98 accuracy 1.00 56962 macro avg 0.98 0.88 0.92 56962 weighted avg 1.00 1.00 1.00 56962
 
Since the class is imbalanced, we clearly cannot use accuracy (value of 1 which is too optimistic) as the evaluation metric. Instead, we will use ROC-AUC evaluation metric.
 
- ### Confusion Matrix
In [82]:
cm_rf = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_rf)
sns.heatmap(cm_rf, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues', xticklabels=['Non-Fraud','Fraud'], yticklabels=['Non-Fraud','Fraud'])
plt.title('Random Forest Confusion Matrix')
plt.show()
 
The confusion matrix provides the model's performance on each class. We see that confusion matrix is not a very good tool to represent the results in the class of highly unbalanced data, because we will actually need a different metrics that accounts in the same time for the selectivity and specificity of the method we are using, so that we minimize in the same time both Type I errors and Type II errors.
 
- ### ROC Curve
In [109]:
fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_test, y_prob_rf)

plt.plot([0,1], [0,1], "k--")  
plt.xlabel("False Positive Rate")
plt.ylabel("True Positive Rate")
plt.title("ROC Curve - Random Forest")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Conclusions



The ROC-AUC comparison shows that all four tree-based models performed well in distinguishing fraudulent from non-fraudulent transactions. Random Forest achieved a test ROC-AUC of 0.957, providing a strong baseline. XGBoost and CatBoost slightly improved on this, with test ROC-AUC scores of 0.968 and 0.972, while LightGBM achieved the highest test ROC-AUC of 0.980. These results indicate that ensemble tree-based models are effective in predicting fraudulent transactions, even with the dataset’s class imbalance.

However, despite the high ROC-AUC values, real-world deployment may still encounter false positives or negatives, especially for rare fraud cases. Overall, LightGBM shows the best performance on this dataset, but all models demonstrate robust predictive ability and could serve as a foundation for practical fraud detection systems.
